clue.text: Writer alarmed, we suspect, about change

indicators.note: to suspect words is to doubt them, so their letters are not to be trusted in the order given
about means going round, so the shuffled letters wrap around the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written, the letters to shuffle
to change something is to alter it

explanation.surface: An author, alarmed at the prospect of change, is suspected by us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we' is fodder, not a link: ALARMED WE rearranged wraps round ALTER to give WALTER DE LA MARE, the English poet of The Listeners.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter de la Mare was an English poet and novelist, best known for verse such as The Listeners.

clue.text: Sweet thing a bit delayed, nymph and company welcomed in

indicators.note: guests welcomed in are taken inside, so these pieces sit within the others

blocks.note: a whit is a tiny bit, as in 'not a whit'
Echo is the nymph of Greek myth who pined for Narcissus
standard abbreviation for company
something delayed arrives late

explanation.surface: A sweet is delayed, and a nymph arrives with company to be welcomed in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit delayed' reads as one phrase meaning slightly late, but its two halves are separate pieces that open to let the others in.
explanation.definitionFit: White chocolate is a confection of cocoa butter, sugar and milk, so it counts as a sweet treat.

clue.text: Upholsterer’s first to stuff stretched seat

indicators.note: first points to the opening letter of the word before it
stuffing something puts filling inside it, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: opening letter of the tradesman's name
something stretched has been made longer

explanation.surface: An upholsterer begins by stuffing padding into a long reclining seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A lounger is a reclining chair or sunbed, a piece of furniture for sitting or lying on.

clue.text: Artist partial to modern style

indicators.note: partial means only part of the following words is used, so a run of letters is taken from them

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A painter who is fond of contemporary fashion in art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partial to' looks like 'fond of', but it means only part of the next words is taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a German painter and sculptor, a leading figure in Dada and Surrealism.

clue.text: Educational initiatives creating openings, accomplished performance coming first

indicators.note: openings are starts, so only the opening letters of the two words before are used
says these pieces are placed ahead of the selected letters

blocks.note: to accomplish a task is to have done or did it
an act is a performance on stage
the starting letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Schemes in schools opening doors, with a fine performance first on the programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Didactic describes something intended to teach or instruct, often with a moral lesson in mind.

clue.text: Little French number, sexy clothes as folly

indicators.note: used as a verb, clothes means covers or dresses, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: lacy underwear is the sexy sort, so the setter takes one as the other
un is French for one, a small number

explanation.surface: A skimpy French number and racy clothes are mocked as sheer folly.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'little number' sounds like a dress, but here it is the French for one. 'clothes' is a verb, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunacy means extreme foolishness or madness, the same sense as folly in everyday speech.

clue.text: Expert almost claiming single bird for bachelor’s friend?

definitions.note: cryptic: the appliance a single man relies on for meals

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter
claiming something takes hold of it, so the shortened word holds the next pieces

blocks.note: a maven is an expert or connoisseur
I is the Roman numeral one
the crow is a common black bird

explanation.surface: An expert nearly grabs a lone bird to serve as a single man's companion.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: a bachelor's best friend is the gadget that heats his ready meals, not a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: A microwave oven heats ready meals fast, so it is the stereotypical kitchen ally of a man living alone.

clue.text: Once more, pay for flight

blocks.note: re- is the prefix meaning again
to treat someone is to pay for their meal or drink

explanation.surface: Someone offers to pick up the bill again for a plane journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests an air ticket, but it is fleeing.
explanation.definitionFit: A retreat is a withdrawal from danger or an enemy, which is what taking flight means.

clue.text: Denser, clownish kind of unexceptional toff

indicators.note: a kind of something is a variant form, so the letters are given in a different version

blocks.note: taken as written, every letter of both words

explanation.surface: A thick, buffoonish sort of ordinary upper-class twit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Denser' and 'clownish' read as descriptions of the toff, but they are the letters to rearrange. A toff is British slang for a posh person.
explanation.definitionFit: A chinless wonder is a British label for an ineffectual, dim member of the upper classes, so a mediocre posh man.

clue.text: I waste old money on old fossil

blocks.note: taken as written
guano is bird or bat droppings, a waste product
d was the abbreviation for the old British penny
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to squandering their savings on a doddery old codger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old fossil' sounds like an insult for an elderly person, but the 'old' belongs to the wordplay. d stood for the pre-1971 British penny.
explanation.definitionFit: The iguanodon is a large plant-eating dinosaur known chiefly from fossil bones found in England and Belgium.

clue.text: Hear contract is secure

blocks.note: first meaning: to make out what is said
second meaning: to come down with an illness
third meaning: to fasten, as with a latch

explanation.surface: A notice that a heard agreement is binding and safe.
explanation.walkthrough: There are three meanings here, not two: 'contract' is the verb for picking up an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers making out speech, picking up an infection, and fastening something with a latch or clasp.

clue.text: Rowing team’s struggle, in first position dropping back a place?

indicators.text: in first position dropping back a place
indicators.note: the opening letter steps back one place in the alphabet and is replaced by its predecessor

blocks.note: a fight is a struggle

explanation.surface: A boat crew's battle, slipping from leading the race to one place behind.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a bumps race; in fact the F of FIGHT becomes E, the letter one back in the alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing boat with eight oarsmen and a cox is called an eight, and so is its crew.

clue.text: Massive storm virtually engulfing tiny seed

indicators.note: virtually means almost entirely, so the word loses its last letter
to engulf is to swallow up, so the shortened word surrounds the other piece

blocks.note: a cyclone is a violent storm
a pea is a small round seed

explanation.surface: A huge storm all but swallows a little seed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyclopean means gigantic, after the one-eyed giants said to have built huge ancient stone walls.

clue.text: Grandad ultimately hampered by grim internet protocol, suffering

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept
something hampered is hemmed in, so the letter sits inside the next word

blocks.note: grim conditions are harsh
the final letter of the word
IP is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Grandpa finally struggles with a grim online connection and suffers for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardship is severe suffering or privation, so the noun suffering stands in for it directly.

clue.text: Framed by possible killer, put on oath

indicators.note: a picture framed is surrounded on all sides, so the next piece goes inside

blocks.note: a sword is a weapon that may kill
to put on clothes is to wear them

explanation.surface: Someone is stitched up by a likely murderer and made to give sworn testimony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on oath' reads as one phrase about a witness; 'put on' is the wordplay and 'oath' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Oath here is a curse or profanity, the sense of a word you swear with in anger.

clue.text: Not only the lining in bloke’s cloak

blocks.note: first meaning: the membrane lining a mollusc's shell
second meaning: a loose sleeveless cape, as a man might wear

explanation.surface: A man's cape has more to it than just its inner lining.
explanation.walkthrough: The frame is 'not only X but also Y'; 'bloke's' hints at the MAN that starts the word.
explanation.definitionFit: In zoology the mantle is the fold of tissue lining a mollusc's shell; in dress it is a loose outer cape.

clue.text: Rescuer, albeit of strays

indicators.note: to stray is to wander off course, so the letters drift out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written, every letter of both words

explanation.surface: A saviour, even if only of lost animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strays' looks like stray animals saved by an animal rescuer, but it is a verb telling the letters to wander.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeboat is a vessel launched to save people in distress at sea, so it acts as a rescuer.

clue.text: College student’s last drink

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: Clare is a Cambridge college
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A university student's final tipple of the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'student' suggests L for learner, but it only supplies its last letter; the college is Clare, at Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret is the British name for red Bordeaux wine, an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Careful to protect British, a Canadian province

indicators.note: protecting something shields it on all sides, so the next piece is placed within

blocks.note: an alert person is watchful and careful
standard abbreviation
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wary of shielding Britain, a Canadian region acts.
explanation.definitionFit: Alberta is one of Canada's ten provinces, in the west, with Edmonton as its capital.

clue.text: Indefatigable, but unable to drive across America?

definitions.note: cryptic: without TIRES, the American spelling of tyres

blocks.note: first meaning: never growing weary
second meaning: read as a car without the US spelling of wheels' rubber rims

explanation.surface: Someone with endless energy who still can't manage a coast-to-coast road trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word: TIRE is the American spelling of tyre, and a car short of them cannot be driven.
explanation.definitionFit: Tireless means never getting weary, which is exactly what indefatigable means.

clue.text: Shave with iodine in Eastern bit of China

indicators.note: in places the element inside the following word

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for east
a plate is a piece of china crockery
I is iodine's chemical symbol

explanation.surface: Someone shaves with iodine somewhere in the eastern part of China.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C of 'China' points to the country; it is lower-case china, crockery.
explanation.definitionFit: To epilate is to remove body hair, a close equivalent of shaving it off.

clue.text: Guy as war hero, flipping great kid

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: great means big
a son is a child

explanation.surface: A soldier-hero is a bloomin' brilliant lad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' looks like a mild British swear word, but it is turning the word over. Guy Gibson led the 1943 Dambusters raid.
explanation.definitionFit: Wing Commander Guy Gibson VC led the Dambusters raid in 1943, making him a famous British war hero.

clue.text: Party whip entire reprobate

indicators.note: to whip is to beat or stir vigorously, so the letters are churned up

blocks.note: Lib is short for the Liberal party
taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A party's whip is a complete scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Party whip' reads as a parliamentary official, but 'whip' is the verb working on the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A libertine is a dissolute person without moral restraint, so a rogue or reprobate.

clue.text: Depart Omani capital — for another?

definitions.note: the capital of a country other than Oman

indicators.note: a capital letter is a word's opening one, so only the first letter is kept

blocks.note: to quit a place is to depart from it
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Leave Muscat, the Omani capital, in exchange for a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' does double duty: it picks the first letter, and with 'for another' it defines a capital other than Oman's. Quito is Ecuador's capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Quito is the capital city of Ecuador, so it is a capital belonging to another nation.

clue.text: Catwoman — or man?

blocks.note: first meaning: a female cat
second meaning: slang for a gay or effeminate man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Catwoman' sounds like the Batman villain, but it is read as a cat who is female.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeding female cat is called a queen, and the word is also slang for a flamboyant gay man.

clue.text: Trunk approximately applied to rear of elephant!

indicators.note: the rear is the back end, so only the final letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: the last letter of the animal
'or so' means approximately, as in ten or so

explanation.surface: An elephant's trunk is roughly attached at its back end, absurdly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunk' suggests the elephant's nose, but it is the human body without head or limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the human trunk, the main part of the body apart from head, arms and legs.

clue.text: It’s namely a record to play with?

definitions.text: It’s namely a record to play with?

indicators.note: something to play with is toyed with and moved about, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: sc. is short for scilicet, Latin for namely
taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about something that is a record you can play with.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: a card kept as a record during play.
explanation.definitionFit: A scorecard records the runs, strokes or points made during a game, so it is a record kept of play.

clue.text: Marmalade lover putting on weight, beginning to bite into fruit

indicators.note: beginning points to the opening letter of the next word
into places the preceding pieces inside the following word

blocks.note: a pear is a fruit
putting on extra is adding it
a ton is a unit of weight
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone fond of marmalade piling on the pounds as they start biting into fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting on weight' reads as getting fat, but splits into two pieces. Paddington is the children's-book bear from Peru who loves marmalade sandwiches.
explanation.definitionFit: Paddington Bear, from Michael Bond's books, famously keeps marmalade sandwiches under his hat.
